group: periodic tape with moving phase defects (Collatz-like growth near 4/3)
title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1LC0LA_---0LD_1LE1RB_0RA0LB_1RE0RE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1LC0LA_---0LD_1LE1RB_0RA0LB_1RE0RE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Read in blocks of 6 cells, the tape is a periodic word with a few phase defects; the head moves them, and the largest block grows by a factor near 4/3 per phase, which suggests a Collatz-like map on the block lengths. The 50 sweep rules used in the first 109 steps are proved in Lean; the accelerated run reaches 9·1011 steps without a halt. The large-scale map has not been found.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 50,991 cells have been visited and 29,836 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.87·10<sup>14</sup> steps (accelerated run)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/py/bbtools/rleaccel.py (blocks of 6 cells, runs crossed in one step, and cycle jumps, each used only after its one-cycle rule has been proved symbolically for all lengths; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 175,400,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt. That is more than 1.87·1014 machine steps; the tape then spans 22,200,732 cells.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.024). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.455).

claims.title: 50 cycle rules
claims.text: The linear cycles (sweeps over blocks of 6-cell words) that bbtools.cycles uses in the first 109 steps, each proved for all values of its counts with an exact step count.

claims.title: No halt in 9·10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: bbtools.cycles on 6-cell blocks, every jump k applications of a proved cycle rule, reaches 906,804,978,838 steps from blank tape without a halt.

claims.title: Growth by about 4/3 per phase
claims.text: The largest block runs 13491, 18582, 24715, 32860, 43683, 58247, 77410, 101379, 134093, 175559, 230878 at the ends of successive phases: a factor between 1.31 and 1.38, with the step count growing by about its square.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The map from one phase to the next (the block lengths between the defects) has not been written down; if it is Collatz-like, as the growth factor near 4/3 suggests, halting would depend on residues of an exponentially growing orbit.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Read in blocks of six cells, this machine's tape is one repeating word with a few places where the pattern slips; the head moves those slips around, and the longest block grows by about a third each time. That is the signature of a Collatz-like map, which has not been pinned down.

facts.text: The sweep rules of the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps, proved in Lean.
No halt, with every jump a proved rule.
Growth of the largest block per phase.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.024). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.455).
After 109 steps the tape spans 50,991 cells (77 left of the start, 34,674 right), with a density of 1s of 0.585.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A periodic word with defects
html: Cut the tape into blocks of 6 cells and almost every block is 110100 or one of its rotations (101001, 010011, …), with some stretches of 110110. Between them sit a few defects where the period slips. At step 906,804,978,838 the tape is

The head sweeps over these blocks; every sweep is a linear cycle, and the 50 cycles used in the first 109 steps are proved in Lean. Over a phase of many sweeps the longest block grows by a factor near 4/3 and the step count by about its square.

sections.heading: Open
html: The machine stops only if the head, in state B and moving left, meets two blank cells in a row. The accelerated run, every jump of which is a proved rule, reaches 9·1011 steps without that happening. Deciding the question would need the map from one phase to the next, which is probably Collatz-like and has not been found.

summary: In 6-cell blocks the tape is the periodic word 110100 with a few phase defects; sweeps move them, and over each phase the largest block grows by about 4/3. 50 cycle rules proved in Lean; no halt in 9*10^11 steps. Large-scale map not found.
